text: Time to put Chapters 13 and 14 together in a full worked lab: finding duplicated logic across real flows, and extracting it into a reusable subflow.

You're the Flow Designer administrator on an instance with three flows already in production: Employee Onboarding, Employee Offboarding, and Equipment Request. Reviewing them, you notice all three contain an identical block built inline, three separate times: notify the employee's manager that a decision is needed, wait for that manager to respond, and log the decision and a timestamp onto the triggering record. The only real differences between the three copies are which record each flow is working with and the exact notification wording -- both just data, not logic. That's the signal this is safe to extract.

Before touching Flow Designer, design what the subflow needs. Three Inputs: Manager, a reference to the sys underscore user who gets notified; Request Record, a reference to whichever record the decision applies to; and Message, a string, since the wording differs slightly across the three callers. Two Outputs: Decision, approved or rejected, and Decision Date, when that decision was made.

Now build it. Create a new flow record flagged as a Subflow, named Notify and Log Manager Decision, with those inputs and outputs defined on it. Build the body exactly once -- notify, wait, log the result into the two outputs. Then go back to each of the three original flows: delete the duplicated inline block, drop in a single Call Subflow action, and map that flow's own manager, record, and message into the subflow's inputs. Wherever the old inline block used to feed a later step, swap in the subflow's new Decision and Decision Date outputs instead, now available as data pills right after the call.

Run each of the three flows against a test record. The expected result is that nothing about their behavior changed -- same notification, same logged decision, same date -- because only where the logic lives changed, not what it does. A fourth flow that needs this same behavior now just calls the subflow; no copying required. Next, Chapter 5 opens with triggering a flow from a Catalog Item request.
